statement: For integers $n \ge 0$ and $k \ge n+2$, the forgetful functor from [k-tuply monoidal n-categories](c:k-tuply-monoidal-n-category) to $(n+2)$-tuply monoidal $n$-categories is an [equivalence](c:equivalence-of-categories). Here a $k$-tuply monoidal $n$-category is an $E_k$-algebra in the $(n+1)$-category of [n-categories](c:n-category).

hypotheses.text: The integers satisfy $n \ge 0$ and $k \ge n+2$.

conclusion: The forgetful functor from $k$-tuply monoidal $n$-categories to $(n+2)$-tuply monoidal $n$-categories is an equivalence.

proofs.name: Truncated little cubes
proofs.slogan: Algebras in an $(n+1)$-category see only the $n$-truncation of the little cubes operad, and the truncations of $E_k$ agree for $k \ge n+2$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline: the steps follow Lurie's argument, which Gepner and Haugseng carry out for enriched $\infty$-categories. The operadic lemmas themselves are in the cited paper.

roles.why: The bound $k \ge n+2$ makes the configuration spaces $n$-connected, so $n$-truncation erases the difference between $E_{n+2}$ and $E_k$.

steps.slogan: Write [k-tuply monoidal n-categories](c:k-tuply-monoidal-n-category) as $E_k$-algebras in the $(n+1)$-category of $n$-categories.
steps.detail: Gepner and Haugseng build [n-categories](c:n-category) by iterated enrichment. They form an $\infty$-category whose mapping spaces, the cores of functor categories, are $n$-truncated. A $k$-tuply monoidal $n$-category is an algebra over the [little cubes operad](c:little-cubes-operad) $E_k$ in it, and forgetting down to $E_{n+2}$ is restriction along $E_{n+2} \to E_k$.

steps.slogan: Show that every configuration space of points in $\mathbb{R}^k$ is $(k-2)$-connected.
steps.detail: The space of $m$ ordered points in $\mathbb{R}^k$ fibres over the space of $m-1$ points, with fibre $\mathbb{R}^k$ minus $m-1$ points, a wedge of $(k-1)$-spheres. Induction on $m$ shows that the [configuration space of points](c:configuration-space-of-points) is $(k-2)$-connected.

steps.slogan: Show that an algebra structure in an $(n+1)$-category depends only on the $n$-truncated operad.
steps.detail: The operations of an operad $O$ act through maps from the spaces $O(m)$ into mapping spaces of the target. These mapping spaces are $n$-truncated, so each map factors through the [truncation](c:truncation) of $O(m)$. The cited paper makes this precise: algebras over $O$ and over its $n$-truncation agree.

steps.slogan: Show that $E_{n+2} \to E_k$ becomes an equivalence after $n$-truncation.
steps.detail: For $k \ge n+2$, both $\mathrm{Conf}_m(\mathbb{R}^{n+2})$ and $\mathrm{Conf}_m(\mathbb{R}^k)$ are $n$-connected by the previous step, so their $n$-truncations are contractible. Hence the map between them is an equivalence on $n$-truncations in every arity $m$.

steps.slogan: Restrict algebras along the truncated equivalence to get an equivalence of algebra categories.
steps.detail: Restriction along an equivalence of operads is an equivalence of algebra categories. By the truncation step, algebras over $E_k$ and over $E_{n+2}$ in the $\infty$-category of $n$-categories are algebras over equivalent operads. So the forgetful functor between them is an [equivalence](c:equivalence-of-categories).

concepts.c:k-tuply-monoidal-n-category: These are the algebras whose forgetful functor the theorem compares.
concepts.c:equivalence-of-categories: The theorem asserts that the forgetful functor is an equivalence.
concepts.c:n-category: The target is the category of n-categories, whose mapping spaces are truncated.
concepts.c:little-cubes-operad: Its algebras are the k-tuply monoidal structures.
concepts.c:configuration-space-of-points: These spaces are the operations of the little cubes operad.
concepts.c:truncation: Truncation removes the part of the operad that n-categories cannot see.

source.ref: D. Gepner and R. Haugseng, Enriched infinity-categories via non-symmetric infinity-operads, Advances in Mathematics 279 (2015), 575-716
source.note: The paper derives the stabilization hypothesis from Lurie's argument for (n,1)-categories; the outline follows that argument.

statement: Let $u\colon C \to D$ be a [fully faithful](c:fully-faithful-infinity-1-functor) functor of $\infty$-categories, with $C$ small, a topology $\tau$ on $C$ and a topology $\rho$ on $D$, satisfying conditions (a) to (c) below. Then restriction along $u$ is an equivalence from $\rho$-[sheaves](c:infinity-1-sheaf) on $D$ to $\tau$-sheaves on $C$.

hypotheses.text: The functor $u$ is [fully faithful](c:fully-faithful-infinity-1-functor), $C$ is small and $D$ is locally small.
(a) Every $\tau$-[covering sieve](c:covering-sieve) is generated by a family $\{U_i \to X\}$ whose fibre products exist and are preserved by $u$, and $\{uU_i \to uX\}$ is a $\rho$-cover.
(b) For $X$ in $C$ and every $\rho$-covering sieve $R$ on $uX$, the pullback $u^*R$ is a $\tau$-covering sieve on $X$.
(c) Every object of $D$ has a $\rho$-cover whose fibre products exist and lie in the essential image of $u$.

conclusion: Restriction along $u$ gives an equivalence from $\rho$-sheaves on $D$ to $\tau$-sheaves on $C$.

proofs.name: Restriction and right Kan extension
proofs.slogan: Show that restriction and right Kan extension along $u$ preserve sheaves and that the unit and counit are equivalences on sheaves.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, as an outline of the standard comparison-lemma argument; Hoyois states the conditions precisely in his Lemma C.3. The sheaves are sheaves of spaces on $\infty$-categories with topologies.

roles.why: Full faithfulness makes right Kan extension fully faithful, which gives the counit equivalence.
Covers that $u$ carries to covers let a $\rho$-sheaf restrict to a $\tau$-sheaf.
Pulling covering sieves back from $D$ lets a $\tau$-sheaf extend to a $\rho$-sheaf.
Covers by objects in the image of $u$ reduce descent in $D$ to descent in $C$.

steps.slogan: Restrict and extend [presheaves](c:infinity-1-presheaf) along the fully faithful functor $u$.
steps.detail: Restriction $u^*$ from presheaves on $D$ to presheaves on $C$ has a right adjoint $u_*$, the right Kan extension. Because $u$ is fully faithful, $u^*u_* \simeq \mathrm{id}$. So $u_*$ is fully faithful and the counit is an equivalence.

steps.slogan: Show that $u^*$ sends $\rho$-sheaves to $\tau$-sheaves.
steps.detail: Let $F$ be a $\rho$-sheaf and $\{U_i \to X\}$ a generating cover from (a). The images $uU_i$ form a $\rho$-cover of $uX$ with the same fibre products. So descent for $F$ along it is descent for $u^*F$ along $\{U_i\}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $u_*$ sends $\tau$-sheaves to $\rho$-sheaves.
steps.detail: For $X$ in $C$, $u_*G(uX)=G(X)$, and by (b) a $\rho$-sieve on $uX$ pulls back to a $\tau$-sieve. So descent for $u_*G$ at $uX$ is descent for $G$. For general $Y$, a $\rho$-cover of $Y$ from (c) reduces the claim to objects in the image of $u$.

steps.slogan: Show that the unit $F \to u_*u^*F$ is an equivalence for every $\rho$-sheaf $F$.
steps.detail: Choose a $\rho$-cover $\{V_j \to Y\}$ as in (c). Both $F(Y)$ and $u_*u^*F(Y)$ are limits over its \v{C}ech nerve. The two limits agree because the unit is an equivalence at objects in the image of $u$.

steps.slogan: Combine the unit and counit equivalences into an equivalence of sheaf categories.
steps.detail: On $\tau$-sheaves the counit is an equivalence by the first step, and on $\rho$-sheaves the unit is an equivalence by the previous step. So $u^* \dashv u_*$ restricts to an equivalence $\mathrm{Shv}_\rho(D) \simeq \mathrm{Shv}_\tau(C)$, and $u(C)$ is a [dense subsite](c:dense-sub-site).

concepts.c:fully-faithful-infinity-1-functor: Full faithfulness makes the right Kan extension fully faithful.
concepts.c:infinity-1-sheaf: The lemma compares the sheaf categories on the two sites.
concepts.c:covering-sieve: Covering sieves state the sheaf condition and the conditions on covers.
concepts.c:infinity-1-presheaf: Presheaves carry the adjunction before one restricts to sheaves.
concepts.c:dense-sub-site: The three conditions say that the image of u is a dense subsite.

source.ref: M. Hoyois, A quadratic refinement of the Grothendieck-Lefschetz-Verdier trace formula, Algebraic & Geometric Topology 14 (2014), 3603-3658, Lemma C.3
source.note: Hoyois proves the comparison lemma for sheaves of spaces on infinity-categories with topologies; the outline gives the shape of that argument.

statement: Let $M$ be a cusped [hyperbolic 3-manifold](c:hyperbolic-3-manifold) with disjoint horoball neighbourhoods of its [cusps](c:cusp). If slopes $s_1,\dots,s_k$ on $k$ of the boundary tori each have length greater than $2\pi$ in the Euclidean metric of the torus, then the [Dehn filling](c:dehn-filling) $M(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ has a complete Riemannian metric of negative sectional curvature.

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is a complete cusped [hyperbolic 3-manifold](c:hyperbolic-3-manifold) with disjoint horoball neighbourhoods of its cusps.
Each slope $s_i$ on the boundary torus $T_i$ of a chosen cusp neighbourhood has length greater than $2\pi$.

conclusion: The Dehn filling $M(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ carries a complete Riemannian metric of negative sectional curvature.

proofs.name: Warped metric on the cusp collars
proofs.slogan: Replace the hyperbolic metric in each filled cusp neighbourhood by a negatively curved warped metric that closes up the filling solid torus.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline: the construction is due to Gromov and Thurston, and Bleiler and Hodgson give the details. The collars are disjoint, so the filled cusps are treated one at a time, and unfilled cusps keep the complete hyperbolic metric.

roles.why: Each cusp neighbourhood has the explicit metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}h_T$, which the proof replaces by a warped metric.
Length greater than $2\pi$ is exactly what lets a convex profile close up with slope one.

steps.slogan: Write each [cusp](c:cusp) neighbourhood as a flat torus times a half-line with an explicit metric.
steps.detail: A horoball neighbourhood of a cusp is $T \times [0,\infty)$ with metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}h_T$, where $h_T$ is the flat metric of the horospherical torus $T$. Take coordinates $\theta$ along the slope $s$, scaled to period $2\pi$, and $t$ orthogonal to it.

steps.slogan: Replace the metric on a collar by the warped product $dr^2+f(r)^2d\theta^2+g(r)^2dt^2$.
steps.detail: The hyperbolic metric has $f(r)=(\ell/2\pi)e^{-r}$ and $g(r)=c\,e^{-r}$, where $\ell>2\pi$ is the length of $s$. The coordinate planes of such a metric have curvatures $-f''/f$, $-g''/g$ and $-f'g'/(fg)$.

steps.slogan: Choose convex decreasing profiles $f$ and $g$ that close the $\theta$-circle smoothly.
steps.detail: Let $f$ and $g$ equal the hyperbolic profiles near $r=0$, with $f''>0$, $g''>0$ and $f',g'<0$. Require $f(R)=0$, $f'(R)=-1$ and $g'(R)=0$. A convex $f$ can drop from slope $-\ell/2\pi$ to slope $-1$ exactly because $\ell/2\pi>1$.

steps.slogan: Check that the metric extends smoothly over the solid torus glued along the slope.
steps.detail: At $r=R$ the $\theta$-circle shrinks to a point. The conditions $f(R)=0$ and $f'(R)=-1$, with $f$ odd and $g$ even about $R$, make the metric smooth there. The collar closes up to a solid torus with meridian $s$, so the manifold is the [Dehn filling](c:dehn-filling).

steps.slogan: Show that every plane has negative sectional curvature on the filled solid torus.
steps.detail: In the frame $\partial_r,\partial_\theta,\partial_t$ the curvature operator is diagonal, so the [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature) of a plane is a convex combination of the three coordinate curvatures. All three are negative, and the limit at the core is $-g''(R)/g(R)<0$. Elsewhere the metric is hyperbolic and complete.

concepts.c:hyperbolic-3-manifold: The manifold M carries the hyperbolic metric that the proof modifies.
concepts.c:cusp: The modification takes place in the cusp neighbourhoods.
concepts.c:dehn-filling: The filled solid torus is glued in along the chosen slope.
concepts.c:sectional-curvature: Negative sectional curvature of the new metric is the goal.

source.ref: M. Gromov and W. Thurston, Pinching constants for hyperbolic manifolds, Inventiones Mathematicae 89 (1987), 1-12; details in S. A. Bleiler and C. D. Hodgson, Spherical space forms and Dehn filling, Topology 35 (1996), 809-833
source.note: The outline follows the warped-product construction of the cusp collars in those papers.

statement: For an integer $m \ge 0$ and numbers $w \ne 0$ and $z$, the sum $\sum_{k=0}^{m}\binom{m}{k}(w+m-k)^{m-k-1}(z+k)^{k}$ of shifted [binomial coefficient](c:binomial-coefficient) terms equals $w^{-1}(z+w+m)^{m}$.

hypotheses.text: The number $m$ is a nonnegative integer.
The numbers $w$ and $z$ lie in a field of characteristic $0$, and $w \ne 0$.

proofs.name: Tree function and Lagrange inversion
proofs.slogan: Expand two exponentials of the tree function by Lagrange inversion, multiply the series, and compare coefficients.
proofs.scope: The whole identity. Multiplying by $w$ gives a polynomial identity in $w$ and $z$ with rational coefficients, which the series argument proves, so it holds in every field of characteristic $0$.

roles.why: The integer $m$ indexes the coefficient of $t^m$ that is compared.
Dividing the polynomial identity by $w \ne 0$ gives the stated form.

steps.slogan: Define the tree function $T(t)$ by the equation $T=te^{T}$.
steps.detail: The equation $T=te^{T}$ has a unique solution in the ring of [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) $\mathbb{Q}[[t]]$ with $T(0)=0$. It is the [generating function](c:generating-function) $\sum n^{n-1}t^n/n!$ of [rooted trees](c:rooted-tree), but only the equation is used.

steps.slogan: Expand $e^{xT}$ by Lagrange inversion to get $\sum_n x(x+n)^{n-1}t^n/n!$.
steps.detail: For $T=t\varphi(T)$, Lagrange inversion gives $[t^n]H(T)=[u^n]\,H(u)\varphi(u)^n(1-u\varphi'(u)/\varphi(u))$. With $\varphi=e^u$ and $H=e^{xu}$ this is $[u^n]e^{(x+n)u}(1-u)=(x+n)^n/n!-(x+n)^{n-1}/(n-1)!=x(x+n)^{n-1}/n!$.

steps.slogan: Expand $e^{zT}/(1-T)$ the same way to get $\sum_n (z+n)^n t^n/n!$.
steps.detail: Take $H=e^{zu}/(1-u)$ in the same formula with $\varphi=e^u$. Then $H(u)\varphi(u)^n(1-u)=e^{(z+n)u}$, and its $u^n$-coefficient is $(z+n)^n/n!$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the two series and merge the exponentials.
steps.detail: Since $e^{wT}\cdot e^{zT}/(1-T)=e^{(w+z)T}/(1-T)$, the expansions give $\sum_n (w+z+n)^n t^n/n!=\bigl(\sum_j w(w+j)^{j-1}t^j/j!\bigr)\bigl(\sum_i (z+i)^i t^i/i!\bigr)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $t^m$ and divide by $w$.
steps.detail: The coefficient of $t^m/m!$ gives $\sum_{j}\binom{m}{j}\,w(w+j)^{j-1}(z+m-j)^{m-j}=(w+z+m)^m$, a polynomial identity in $w$ and $z$ (the term $j=0$ is $(z+m)^m$). Divide by $w \ne 0$ and put $j=m-k$.

concepts.c:binomial-coefficient: The terms of the sum carry the binomial coefficients that the product of series produces.
concepts.c:formal-power-series: All series are formal, so no convergence question arises.
concepts.c:generating-function: The identity is read off from coefficients of generating functions.
concepts.c:rooted-tree: The tree function counts rooted trees and satisfies the tree equation.

source.note: The standard Lagrange inversion proof of Abel's identity; see R. P. Stanley, Enumerative Combinatorics, volume 2, chapter 5.

statement: The Anderson spectrum $I_{\mathbb Z}$, the fibre of $I_{\mathbb Q}\to I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}$, gives each [spectrum](c:stable-homotopy-type) $X$ a natural exact sequence $0\to \mathrm{Ext}(\pi_{n-1}X,\mathbb Z)\to I_{\mathbb Z}^n(X)\to \mathrm{Hom}(\pi_nX,\mathbb Z)\to 0$. If the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group-of-a-spectrum) of $X$ are finitely generated, then $X\to I_{\mathbb Z}I_{\mathbb Z}X$ is an equivalence.

hypotheses.text: The object $X$ is a [spectrum](c:stable-homotopy-type).
For the duality statement, every homotopy group of $X$ is a [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-group) abelian group.

conclusion: The sequence holds for every spectrum, and the double dual map is an equivalence when the homotopy groups are finitely generated, so $I_{\mathbb Z}$ is a dualizing object there.

proofs.name: Universal coefficient sequence
proofs.slogan: Build $I_{\mathbb Z}$ from the rational and the Brown-Comenetz spectra, read the sequence off a long exact sequence, and compare the unit with it.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Here $I_A$ is the spectrum with $I_A^n(X)=\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_nX,A)$ for $A=\mathbb Q,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$, and $I_{\mathbb Z}X$ is the function spectrum $F(X,I_{\mathbb Z})$.

roles.why: The representing spectra and the long exact sequence are built for an arbitrary spectrum $X$.
Finite generation makes Hom into $\mathbb Z$ free and Ext finite, so the double dual is computed by the sequence.

steps.slogan: Represent $X\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_0X,A)$ by a spectrum $I_A$ for $A=\mathbb{Q}$ and $A=\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$.
steps.detail: The groups $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ are [injective](c:injective-module), so the functor sends cofibre sequences to exact sequences and wedges to products. Brown representability gives spectra $I_{\mathbb Q}$ and $I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}$, the second the Brown-Comenetz spectrum, with $I_A^n(X)=\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_nX,A)$.

steps.slogan: Form $I_{\mathbb Z}$ as the fibre of the map $I_{\mathbb Q}\to I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}$ induced by $\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$.
steps.detail: The quotient map induces a natural map of the represented functors, hence a map of spectra by Yoneda. Its fibre gives, for each $X$, a long [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) $I_{\mathbb Q}^{n-1}X\to I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}^{n-1}X\to I_{\mathbb Z}^nX\to I_{\mathbb Q}^nX\to I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}^nX$.

steps.slogan: Read the short exact sequence for $I_{\mathbb Z}^n(X)$ off the long exact sequence.
steps.detail: Let $A=\pi_{n-1}X$ and $B=\pi_nX$. Since $\mathrm{Ext}(A,\mathbb Q)=0$, the sequence $0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Q\to\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\to0$ shows that $\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb Q)\to\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ has cokernel $\mathrm{Ext}(A,\mathbb Z)$, and that $\mathrm{Hom}(B,\mathbb Q)\to\mathrm{Hom}(B,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ has kernel $\mathrm{Hom}(B,\mathbb Z)$. The long sequence is then the claimed short one, with [Ext](c:ext-group) as stated.

steps.slogan: Compute the homotopy groups of the dual $I_{\mathbb Z}X$ and of the double dual.
steps.detail: Since $\pi_kI_{\mathbb Z}X=I_{\mathbb Z}^{-k}X$, the sequence makes it an extension of $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_{-k}X,\mathbb Z)$ by $\mathrm{Ext}(\pi_{-k-1}X,\mathbb Z)$. For finitely generated groups the Hom is free and the Ext is finite, so $Y=I_{\mathbb Z}X$ again has finitely generated homotopy. Applied to $Y$, the sequence gives $\pi_kI_{\mathbb Z}Y$ as an extension of $\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_kX,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$ by $\mathrm{Ext}(\mathrm{Ext}(\pi_kX,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the unit map $X\to I_{\mathbb Z}I_{\mathbb Z}X$ with these extensions by the five lemma.
steps.detail: For a finitely generated group $A$, the maps $A/\mathrm{tors}\to\mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Hom}(A,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$ and $\mathrm{tors}\,A\to\mathrm{Ext}(\mathrm{Ext}(A,\mathbb Z),\mathbb Z)$ are isomorphisms. The unit is compatible with the two natural sequences and induces these maps, so it is an isomorphism on every $\pi_k$, hence an equivalence.

concepts.c:stable-homotopy-type: The statement lives in the homotopy category of spectra.
concepts.c:homotopy-group-of-a-spectrum: The sequence and the finiteness condition concern these groups.
concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finite generation makes the double dual of each homotopy group computable.
concepts.c:injective-module: Injectivity of Q and Q/Z makes Hom into them exact.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: The long exact sequence of the fibre gives the universal coefficient sequence.
concepts.c:ext-group: The Ext term measures the torsion of the homotopy groups.

source.note: Anderson's universal coefficient theorem (D. W. Anderson, 1969 notes), proved here from Brown-Comenetz duality and the five lemma.

statement: Let $ABCD$ be a convex [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) that is not a parallelogram, let $E$ and $F$ be the midpoints of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$, and let $P$ be an interior point. Then $[ABP]+[CDP]=[BCP]+[DAP]$ if and only if $P$ lies on the line $EF$. In that case both sums are half the [area](c:area) of $ABCD$.

hypotheses.text: The [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) $ABCD$ is convex, with its vertices in counterclockwise order.
The quadrilateral $ABCD$ is not a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram).
The point $P$ lies in the interior of $ABCD$.

conclusion: The two sums of triangle areas are equal exactly when $P$ lies on the Newton line $EF$, and then each sum is half the area of $ABCD$.

proofs.name: Signed areas are affine
proofs.slogan: The difference of the two area sums is an affine function of $P$ that vanishes at $E$, so it vanishes exactly on the line $EF$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in both directions. For a parallelogram $E=F$ and every interior point satisfies the equality, which is why that case is excluded.

roles.why: Convexity makes the four triangles around an interior point tile $ABCD$ with positive orientation.
An interior point gives four triangles whose signed and ordinary areas agree.
The diagonals of a non-parallelogram have different midpoints, so $E\ne F$ and the zero set is a line.

steps.slogan: Define $f(P)=[ABP]+[CDP]-[BCP]-[DAP]$ with signed areas $[XYZ]=\tfrac12\det(Y-X,Z-X)$.
steps.detail: For $P$ inside the convex [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) with counterclockwise labels, all four signed areas are positive and equal the ordinary areas. So $f(P)$ is the difference of the two area sums, and the theorem asks when $f(P)=0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f$ is affine in $P$ with linear part $2\det(F-E,P)$.
steps.detail: Each signed area $[XYP]$ is affine in $P$ with linear part $\tfrac12\det(Y-X,P)$. The linear parts add up to $\tfrac12\det\bigl((B-A)+(D-C)-(C-B)-(A-D),P\bigr)=\det(B+D-A-C,P)=2\det(F-E,P)$, because $E=(A+C)/2$ and $F=(B+D)/2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f(E)=0$ because $E$ is the midpoint of $AC$.
steps.detail: Triangles $ABE$ and $CBE$ have equal bases $AE=EC$ and the common apex $B$, so $[ABE]=[BCE]$. In the same way $[CDE]=[DAE]$. Hence $f(E)=0$.

steps.slogan: Solve $f(P)=0$: it holds exactly on the line through $E$ and $F$.
steps.detail: The two previous steps give $f(P)=2\det(F-E,P-E)$. The diagonals of a non-parallelogram do not bisect each other, so $E\ne F$. Then $f(P)=0$ exactly when $P-E$ is parallel to $F-E$, that is, when $P$ lies on the line $EF$.

steps.slogan: Show that the two equal sums are each half the area of $ABCD$.
steps.detail: For interior $P$ the four triangles tile $ABCD$, so the two sums add up to its [area](c:area). They are equal exactly when each is half of it. By the first step this is $f(P)=0$, which holds exactly for $P$ on $EF$.

concepts.c:quadrilateral: The theorem concerns the four triangles cut from a convex quadrilateral.
concepts.c:area: Equality of area sums is the property that the Newton line characterizes.
concepts.c:parallelogram: A parallelogram has equal midpoints of diagonals, so it is the excluded case.

source.note: The signed-area argument, in which the area difference is an affine function of P; the statement is Anne's theorem on the Newton line of a quadrilateral.

statement: For $n \ge 0$, the Aztec diamond $A_n$ is the union of the unit squares with centres $(x,y)\in(\mathbb Z+\tfrac12)^2$ and $|x|+|y|\le n$. It has exactly $2^{n(n+1)/2}$ [domino tilings](c:domino-tiling).

hypotheses.text: The order $n$ is a nonnegative integer.

conclusion: The number of domino tilings of $A_n$ is $2^{n(n+1)/2}$.

proofs.name: Graphical condensation
proofs.slogan: Kuo's condensation gives $a_na_{n-2}=2a_{n-1}^2$ for the tiling numbers $a_n$, and induction solves this recurrence.
proofs.scope: All $n\ge0$: the cases $n=0,1$ are counted directly and $n\ge2$ follows by induction. A tiling of $A_n$ is a [perfect matching](c:perfect-matching) of the dual graph.

roles.why: The order $n$ is the induction parameter, and the two smallest orders start the induction.

steps.slogan: Count the tilings of $A_0$ and $A_1$ directly.
steps.detail: The diamond $A_0$ is empty and has one tiling. The diamond $A_1$ is a $2\times2$ square and has two tilings. So $a_0=1=2^0$ and $a_1=2=2^1$.

steps.slogan: Apply Kuo's condensation to the dual graph $G_n$ and its four corner squares $a,b,c,d$.
steps.detail: A tiling of $A_n$ is a [perfect matching](c:perfect-matching) of the planar [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) $G_n$ whose vertices are the squares. Let $a,b,c,d$ be the squares with centres $(\tfrac12,n-\tfrac12)$, $(-n+\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, $(-\tfrac12,-n+\tfrac12)$, $(n-\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)$. They lie on the outer face in this order and alternate in colour, so Kuo's theorem gives $M(G)M(G-\{a,b,c,d\})=M(G-\{a,b\})M(G-\{c,d\})+M(G-\{a,d\})M(G-\{b,c\})$, where $M$ counts perfect matchings.

steps.slogan: Remove two adjacent corners and strip the forced dominoes to reach a copy of $A_{n-1}$.
steps.detail: After deleting two adjacent corner squares, the squares on the boundary staircases beside them each have one free neighbour, so their dominoes are forced one after another. Exactly $2n-1$ dominoes are forced and the remaining squares form a translate of $A_{n-1}$. So each of the four graphs $G-\{a,b\}$, $G-\{c,d\}$, $G-\{a,d\}$, $G-\{b,c\}$ has $a_{n-1}$ tilings.

steps.slogan: Remove all four corners and strip the forced dominoes to reach a copy of $A_{n-2}$.
steps.detail: With all four corners deleted, the same forcing along the four staircases fixes $4n-4$ dominoes and leaves a translate of $A_{n-2}$. So $G-\{a,b,c,d\}$ has $a_{n-2}$ tilings, for $n\ge2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the counts into $a_na_{n-2}=2a_{n-1}^2$ and solve it by induction.
steps.detail: Kuo's identity becomes $a_na_{n-2}=2a_{n-1}^2$. If $a_{n-1}=2^{n(n-1)/2}$ and $a_{n-2}=2^{(n-1)(n-2)/2}$, then $a_n=2^{1+n(n-1)-(n-1)(n-2)/2}=2^{n(n+1)/2}$. Induction from $n=0,1$ gives every $n$.

concepts.c:domino-tiling: The theorem counts these tilings of the Aztec diamond.
concepts.c:perfect-matching: A domino tiling is the same as a perfect matching of the dual graph.
concepts.c:bipartite-graph: The dual graph is bipartite by the checkerboard colouring, as Kuo's theorem requires.

source.note: Kuo's graphical condensation proves the recurrence a_n a_{n-2} = 2 a_{n-1}^2; the steps follow that proof. The theorem is due to Elkies, Kuperberg, Larsen and Propp.

statement: Let $D$ be a [Hermitian symmetric space](c:hermitian-symmetric-space) of noncompact type, realized as a bounded symmetric domain, and let $\Gamma$ be an [arithmetic group](c:arithmetic-group) acting on $D$. Then $\Gamma\backslash D$ has a [compactification](c:compactification) $(\Gamma\backslash D)^*$ that is a normal [projective variety](c:projective-variety) containing $\Gamma\backslash D$ as a Zariski open dense subvariety.

hypotheses.text: The space $D$ is a [Hermitian symmetric space](c:hermitian-symmetric-space) of noncompact type, that is, a bounded symmetric domain.
The group $\Gamma$ is an [arithmetic](c:arithmetic-group) subgroup of the group of holomorphic automorphisms of $D$.

conclusion: The quotient $\Gamma\backslash D$ is an open dense subset of a normal projective variety $(\Gamma\backslash D)^*$ that compactifies it, with boundary a finite union of quotients of rational boundary components.

proofs.name: Satake topology and Poincare series
proofs.slogan: Add the rational boundary components, show that the quotient is compact, and embed it in projective space by automorphic forms of large weight.
proofs.scope: An outline of the construction and of the proof that it has the stated properties; the details are in Baily and Borel's paper. Arithmetic means arithmetic in $G(\mathbb Q)$ for a $\mathbb Q$-form $G$ of the automorphism group of $D$.

roles.why: The boundary components and the Poincare series are built from the geometry of the bounded symmetric domain $D$.
Arithmeticity of $\Gamma$ gives reduction theory, which makes the quotient compact.

steps.slogan: Adjoin the rational boundary components of $D$ with the Satake topology to form $D^*$.
steps.detail: The bounded domain $D$ has boundary components in its closure, and the rational ones are those whose stabilizers are defined over $\mathbb Q$. Adding them to $D$ with the Satake topology gives a space $D^*$ on which $\Gamma$ acts continuously.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Gamma\backslash D^*$ is a compact Hausdorff [compactification](c:compactification) of $\Gamma\backslash D$ by reduction theory.
steps.detail: Borel's reduction theory covers $D$ by finitely many $\Gamma$-translates of Siegel sets. The behaviour of Siegel sets near rational boundary components shows that $\Gamma\backslash D^*$ is compact and Hausdorff, and contains $\Gamma\backslash D$ as an open dense subset.

steps.slogan: Give the quotient the structure of a normal complex analytic space using automorphic forms.
steps.detail: Baily and Borel define the analytic structure of $\Gamma\backslash D^*$ near the boundary through automorphic forms, in the manner of Satake. They prove that this makes it a normal [complex analytic space](c:complex-analytic-space) that extends the complex structure of $\Gamma\backslash D$.

steps.slogan: Construct [automorphic forms](c:automorphic-form) of large weight by relative Poincare series.
steps.detail: Poincare series of high weight, built on $D$ and on the rational boundary components, give automorphic forms that separate points and tangent vectors of $\Gamma\backslash D^*$. They define a holomorphic embedding of the quotient into projective space.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the image is a normal projective variety containing $\Gamma\backslash D$ as an open dense subset.
steps.detail: The image of the embedding is a closed analytic subset of projective space, hence algebraic by Chow's theorem. The ring of automorphic forms is finitely generated and the compactification is its $\mathrm{Proj}$. The boundary is Zariski closed, so $\Gamma\backslash D$ is Zariski open and dense.

concepts.c:hermitian-symmetric-space: The space D is the Hermitian symmetric space whose quotient is compactified.
concepts.c:arithmetic-group: Arithmeticity of the group gives the reduction theory behind compactness.
concepts.c:compactification: The construction adds the rational boundary components to the quotient.
concepts.c:projective-variety: The final compactification is a projective variety.
concepts.c:complex-analytic-space: The compactification first gets a complex analytic structure.
concepts.c:automorphic-form: Automorphic forms of large weight give the projective embedding.

source.ref: W. L. Baily Jr. and A. Borel, Compactification of arithmetic quotients of bounded symmetric domains, Annals of Mathematics 84 (1966), 442-528
source.note: The outline follows the paper: Satake topology on D*, compactness by reduction theory, analytic structure, then the projective embedding by Poincare series.

statement: Let $A$ be a ring, $f\in A$ a nonzerodivisor and $\hat A$ the $f$-adic [completion](c:completion). Then $M\mapsto(M[1/f],M\otimes_A\hat A)$ is an equivalence from $f$-torsion-free $A$-[modules](c:module) to triples $(M_1,M_2,\varphi)$: $M_1$ an $A[1/f]$-module, $M_2$ an $f$-torsion-free $\hat A$-module, $\varphi$ an isomorphism of their base changes to $\hat A[1/f]$.

hypotheses.text: The element $f$ is a nonzerodivisor of the ring $A$.
The modules $M$ and $M_2$ have no $f$-torsion: multiplication by $f$ is injective on them.

conclusion: Gluing an $A[1/f]$-module and an $f$-torsion-free $\hat A$-module along $\varphi$ gives an $f$-torsion-free $A$-module, and this inverts the functor.

proofs.name: Gluing by a preimage
proofs.slogan: Glue a triple into the submodule of $M_1$ that $\varphi$ maps into $M_2$, then check the two composites by working modulo powers of $f$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for modules. The sheaf version on a curve follows by applying it to affine opens with a local parameter $f$.

roles.why: A nonzerodivisor $f$ makes $f$ injective on $\hat A$ with $\hat A/f^n=A/f^n$, which gives the vanishing of $\mathrm{Tor}_1^A(P,\hat A)$.
Torsion freeness embeds $M_2$ in $M_2[1/f]$ and lets one divide by powers of $f$.

steps.slogan: Glue the triple into $M=\{m\in M_1:\varphi(m\otimes1)\in M_2\}$.
steps.detail: Because $M_2$ is $f$-torsion-free, $M_2\subset M_2[1/f]$, so $M$ is a well defined submodule of $M_1$ and $f$ is injective on it. For $m_1\in M_1$ some $f^Nm_1$ lies in $M$, so $M[1/f]=M_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M/f^nM\to M_2/f^nM_2$ is an isomorphism for every $n$.
steps.detail: If $\varphi(m)\in f^nM_2$, then $f^{-n}m\in M$, so the map is injective. For surjectivity write $x\in M_2$ as $\sum\varphi(m_i)b_i$ with $b_i\in\hat A[1/f]$. Since $A/f^N=\hat A/f^N$, replacing the $b_i$ by elements of $A$ modulo high powers of $f$ gives $m\in M$ with $\varphi(m)-x\in f^nM_2$.

steps.slogan: Show that $M\otimes_A\hat A$ has no $f$-torsion.
steps.detail: Since $f$ is a nonzerodivisor on $A$ and on $\hat A$, and $\hat A/f=A/f$, we get $\mathrm{Tor}_1^A(P,\hat A)=0$ for every $A/f$-module $P$. Tensor $0\to M\xrightarrow{f}M\to M/f\to0$ with $\hat A$ to see that $f$ is injective on $M\otimes_A\hat A$.

steps.slogan: Prove that the canonical map $\psi\colon M\otimes_A\hat A\to M_2$ is an isomorphism.
steps.detail: After inverting $f$ it is $\varphi$, so $\psi$ is injective, as the source is $f$-torsion-free. It is bijective modulo every $f^n$ by the congruence step. If $f^Nx=\psi(y)$, then $y\in f^N(M\otimes\hat A)$ by bijectivity modulo $f^N$, so $x$ lies in the image because $M_2$ is $f$-torsion-free.

steps.slogan: Check that gluing and the functor are inverse to each other.
steps.detail: The previous steps give triple, then module, then triple, isomorphic to the start. In the other direction let $M$ be $f$-torsion-free and let $m\in M[1/f]$ lie in the image of $M\otimes\hat A$. Then $f^Nm\in M\cap f^N(M\otimes\hat A)=f^NM$, so $m\in M$, and the [descent](c:descent) data recover $M$.

concepts.c:completion: The completion carries the formal neighbourhood that is glued to the open part.
concepts.c:module: The theorem glues modules over the three rings.
concepts.c:descent: The equivalence says that modules descend from the open part and the completion.

source.note: The proof of Beauville and Laszlo, Un lemme de descente, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 320 (1995), 335-340; see also the formal gluing section of the Stacks Project.

statement: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that every [primitive set](c:primitive-set) $A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $n\ge16$ satisfies $\sum_{a\in A}1/a\le C\log n/\sqrt{\log\log n}$. So the [logarithmic density](c:logarithmic-density) of $A$ in $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is at most $C'/\sqrt{\log\log n}$ and tends to $0$.

hypotheses.text: The set $A\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ is [primitive](c:primitive-set): no element of $A$ divides another.
The bound $n$ satisfies $n\ge16$, so $\log\log n>0$.

conclusion: The sum of $1/a$ over $A$ is at most $C\log n/\sqrt{\log\log n}$, so the logarithmic density of $A$ tends to $0$.

proofs.name: Random divisibility chain
proofs.slogan: Run a random chain of prime-power multiplications from $1$; a primitive set meets each chain at most once, which bounds $\sum1/a$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with an absolute constant $C$ that does not depend on $A$. The argument is a chain-counting proof in the style of the Lubell-Yamamoto-Meshalkin inequality, not Behrend's original one.

roles.why: Primitivity makes $A$ an antichain, so one chain meets it at most once.
A large $n$ keeps $\log\log n$ positive, which the final estimate divides by.

steps.slogan: Build a random chain by multiplying by prime powers chosen with weight $1/q^j$.
steps.detail: Let $\Lambda=\sum_{q^j\le n}1/q^j$ over prime powers. Start at $y=1$, and while a prime power $q^j\le n/y$ exists, pick one with probability proportional to $1/q^j$ and replace $y$ by $yq^j$. The normalizing sum is at most $\Lambda$, and the values of $y$ form a chain under [divisibility](c:divisibility) inside $\{1,\dots,n\}$.

steps.slogan: Bound from below the probability $P(a)$ that the chain passes through $a$.
steps.detail: Let $a=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}$ with distinct primes $p_i$. Each of the $r!$ orders of the [prime powers](c:prime-power) $p_i^{e_i}$ is an admissible sequence of steps ending at $a$, and different orders are different outcomes. Each has probability at least $1/(a\Lambda^r)$, so $P(a)\ge r!/(a\Lambda^r)$.

steps.slogan: Use primitivity: one chain meets the primitive set $A$ at most once.
steps.detail: No element of $A$ divides another, so $A$ is an [antichain](c:antichain) for divisibility, while the values of one chain are totally ordered by divisibility. So the events that the chain passes through $a$, for $a\in A$, are disjoint, and $\sum_{a\in A}P(a)\le1$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds into $\sum_{a\in A}1/a\le\max_{r\ge0}\Lambda^r/r!$.
steps.detail: The lower bound gives $1/a\le P(a)\Lambda^r/r!$ with $r$ the number of distinct prime factors of $a$. Hence $\sum_{a\in A}1/a\le\max_r(\Lambda^r/r!)\sum_{a\in A}P(a)\le\max_r\Lambda^r/r!$.

steps.slogan: Estimate $\Lambda$ by Mertens' theorem and the maximum by Stirling's formula.
steps.detail: Mertens' theorem gives $\Lambda=\log\log n+O(1)$, so $e^\Lambda\ll\log n$. For $r\ge\Lambda/2$, Stirling's formula gives $\Lambda^r/r!\le e^\Lambda/\sqrt{\pi\Lambda}$, and smaller $r$ give less. So the sum is at most $C\log n/\sqrt{\log\log n}$, and dividing by $\sum_{a\le n}1/a\sim\log n$ gives [logarithmic density](c:logarithmic-density) $O(1/\sqrt{\log\log n})$.

concepts.c:primitive-set: The theorem bounds the logarithmic size of primitive sets.
concepts.c:logarithmic-density: The final bound is stated as a logarithmic density that tends to zero.
concepts.c:divisibility: The chain is a chain under divisibility.
concepts.c:prime-power: The chain steps multiply by prime powers.
concepts.c:antichain: A primitive set is an antichain, which a chain meets at most once.

source.note: Behrend proved the bound in J. London Math. Soc. 10 (1935), 42-44; this is a short chain-counting proof of the same bound, not his own argument.

statement: Let $(M,g)$ be a connected [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) of dimension $n\ge2$. Every point has a chart in which the [geodesics](c:geodesic) are straight line segments if and only if $g$ has [constant curvature](c:constant-curvature).

hypotheses.text: The pair $(M,g)$ is a connected smooth [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold).
The dimension satisfies $n\ge2$.

conclusion: A chart that straightens all geodesics exists near every point exactly when the sectional curvature is constant.

proofs.name: Projectively flat connection
proofs.slogan: Straight geodesics force Christoffel symbols of the form $\delta\phi+\delta\phi$, whose curvature is isotropic and constant, and the local models give the converse.
proofs.scope: Both directions, in every dimension $n\ge2$. The converse uses the local models: the plane, the sphere and hyperbolic space.

roles.why: The Levi-Civita connection of $g$ makes $\phi$ a gradient and gives the symmetries of the curvature tensor.
The dimension enters through $(n-1)\,d\sigma=0$, which forces $\sigma$ constant only when $n\ge2$.

steps.slogan: Turn straight geodesics into the identity $\Gamma^k_{ij}=\delta^k_i\phi_j+\delta^k_j\phi_i$.
steps.detail: A [geodesic](c:geodesic) that is a straight line has $\ddot x\parallel\dot x$, so $Q^k(\xi)=\Gamma^k_{ij}\xi^i\xi^j$ is parallel to $\xi$ for every $\xi$. Polarize $Q^k\xi^l-Q^l\xi^k=0$ and contract $l$ with $m$ to get $(n+1)\Gamma^k_{ij}=\delta^k_j\Gamma^l_{il}+\delta^k_i\Gamma^l_{jl}$. Then $\phi_i=\Gamma^l_{il}/(n+1)=\partial_i\log\sqrt{|g|}/(n+1)$ is a gradient.

steps.slogan: Compute the curvature as $R^l{}_{ijk}=\delta^l_kP_{ij}-\delta^l_jP_{ik}$ with $P_{ij}=\partial_i\phi_j-\phi_i\phi_j$.
steps.detail: Insert $\Gamma=\delta\phi+\delta\phi$ into $R^l{}_{ijk}=\partial_j\Gamma^l_{ik}-\partial_k\Gamma^l_{ij}+\Gamma^l_{jm}\Gamma^m_{ik}-\Gamma^l_{km}\Gamma^m_{ij}$. The terms with $\partial_j\phi_k-\partial_k\phi_j$ vanish because $\phi$ is a gradient, and the quadratic terms leave $\delta^l_j\phi_i\phi_k-\delta^l_k\phi_i\phi_j$. This is the stated form, and $P$ is symmetric.

steps.slogan: Use the symmetries of the Riemann tensor to get $P=\sigma g$ for a function $\sigma$.
steps.detail: Lower the index: $R_{lijk}=g_{lk}P_{ij}-g_{lj}P_{ik}$. The antisymmetry $R_{lijk}=-R_{iljk}$, contracted with $g^{lk}$, gives $nP_{ij}=g_{ij}\,\mathrm{tr}P$, so $P=\sigma g$ with $\sigma=\mathrm{tr}P/n$. Then $R(X,Y)Y=\sigma(g(X,Y)Y-|Y|^2X)$, so every plane has [sectional curvature](c:sectional-curvature) $K=-\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $P=\sigma g$ and contract to get $(n-1)\,d\sigma=0$.
steps.detail: From the definition of $P$, $\partial_kP_{ij}-\partial_jP_{ik}=\phi_kP_{ij}-\phi_jP_{ik}$. Insert $P=\sigma g$ and $\partial_kg_{ij}=2\phi_kg_{ij}+\phi_ig_{jk}+\phi_jg_{ik}$ to get $\partial_k\sigma\,g_{ij}=\partial_j\sigma\,g_{ik}$. Contraction with $g^{ij}$ gives $(n-1)\partial_k\sigma=0$, so $\sigma$ and $K$ are constant on the connected $M$.

steps.slogan: For [constant curvature](c:constant-curvature) $K$, find charts near each point that straighten the geodesics.
steps.detail: A metric of constant curvature $K$ is locally isometric to the plane, the round sphere or hyperbolic space of that curvature, by Riemann's normal form. Gnomonic projection sends great circles of the sphere to lines. The Klein ball model of hyperbolic space sends geodesics to chords.

steps.slogan: Join the two implications into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Straight geodesics give constant curvature by the first four steps, and constant curvature gives straight geodesics by the model step. So the two conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:riemannian-manifold: The theorem concerns the geodesics and curvature of a Riemannian metric.
concepts.c:geodesic: Straight geodesics are the hypothesis in a chart, and their equation gives the symbols.
concepts.c:constant-curvature: Constant curvature is the property equivalent to straight geodesics.
concepts.c:sectional-curvature: The computation shows that all planes have the same sectional curvature.

source.note: The classical computation with projectively flat connections (Weyl; see Eisenhart, Riemannian Geometry); the theorem is due to Beltrami (1865).

statement: Let $F$ be a [free algebra](c:free-algebra) over a field $k$ and let $u\in F$ be a nonscalar element. Then the [centralizer](c:commutant) of $u$ in $F$ is isomorphic to the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $k[z]$ for some nonscalar $z\in F$.

hypotheses.text: The algebra $F=k\langle X\rangle$ is a [free](c:free-algebra) associative unital algebra over a field $k$.
The element $u$ is not a scalar multiple of $1$.

conclusion: The centralizer of $u$ equals $k[z]$ for some $z\in F\setminus k$.

proofs.name: Weak algorithm and Cohn's lemma
proofs.slogan: Use the weak algorithm to map the centralizer into a polynomial ring in one variable, then show that it is $k[z]$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Bergman's proof as presented in the literature; the lemmas on the weak algorithm are in the cited paper. A scalar $u$ is excluded because its centralizer is all of $F$.

roles.why: The degree function of the free algebra satisfies the weak algorithm, which controls leading terms of commuting elements.
A nonscalar $u$ makes the centralizer larger than $k$, so the homomorphism to $k[t]$ is not constant.

steps.slogan: Put the free algebra in Cohn's setting: the degree function satisfies the weak algorithm.
steps.detail: The free algebra $F$ with its degree function satisfies the weak algorithm, so $F$ is a free ideal ring and a domain whose units are the nonzero scalars. Leading forms of products are products of leading forms.

steps.slogan: Map every finitely generated subalgebra of $F$ other than $k$ to $k[t]$ without collapsing it.
steps.detail: Bergman proves that every finitely generated subalgebra $R\ne k$ of $F$ has an algebra homomorphism $f\colon R\to k[t]$ with $f(R)\ne k$. He obtains it from the weak algorithm and the structure of free ideal rings.

steps.slogan: Use Lueroth's theorem to describe [integrally closed](c:integrally-closed-domain) subalgebras of $k[t]$.
steps.detail: Cohn shows that an integrally closed subalgebra of $k[t]$ other than $k$ is a polynomial ring $k[z]$. The proof uses Lueroth's theorem on subfields of $k(t)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the centralizer is commutative, integrally closed and embeds in $k[t]$.
steps.detail: As the cited works show, the centralizer $C$ of a nonscalar $u$ is commutative and integrally closed. The homomorphism of the second step is injective on it, because its fraction field has transcendence degree one. Cohn's lemma then gives $C=k[z]$.

concepts.c:free-algebra: The theorem is about the centralizer inside a free algebra.
concepts.c:commutant: The centralizer of u is the set of elements that commute with u.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The centralizer turns out to be a polynomial ring in one variable.
concepts.c:integrally-closed-domain: Integral closure lets Cohn's lemma identify subalgebras of k[t].

source.ref: G. M. Bergman, Centralizers in free associative algebras, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 137 (1969), 327-344
source.note: Bergman's proof uses free ideal rings and the n-term weak algorithm; the final step uses a lemma of P. M. Cohn based on Lueroth's theorem.

statement: Let $K$ run through a sequence of [number fields](c:number-field) that are Galois over $\mathbb Q$, of degree $n$ and absolute [discriminant](c:discriminant) $d$, with $n/\log d\to0$. Then $\log(hR)/\log\sqrt d\to1$, where $h$ is the class number and $R$ the [regulator](c:regulator) of $K$.

hypotheses.text: Each field $K$ is a [Galois](c:galois-extension) extension of $\mathbb Q$.
The degrees and discriminants satisfy $n/\log d\to0$ along the sequence.

proofs.name: Residue of the Dedekind zeta function
proofs.slogan: Express $hR$ through the residue of $\zeta_K$ at $1$, then bound that residue above and below by $d^{o(1)}$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Brauer's proof for fields Galois over $\mathbb Q$; the full proof is in Lang's book. For non-Galois fields the theorem needs the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which is not covered here.

roles.why: Galois fields have $\zeta_K$ as a product of Artin $L$-functions, which Brauer's induction theorem controls.
The condition $n/\log d\to0$ makes the factors $e^{O(n)}$ and the residue upper bound $d^{o(1)}$.

steps.slogan: Write $hR$ through the residue of the [Dedekind zeta function](c:dedekind-zeta-function) at $s=1$.
steps.detail: The class number formula gives $\mathrm{Res}_{s=1}\zeta_K(s)=2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2}hR/(w\sqrt d)$. The factors $2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2}$ and $w$ contribute $e^{O(n)}=d^{o(1)}$. So $\log(hR)=\tfrac12\log d+\log\mathrm{Res}\,\zeta_K+o(\log d)$, and it remains to show $\log\mathrm{Res}\,\zeta_K=o(\log d)$.

steps.slogan: Bound the residue from above using the functional equation and the Euler product.
steps.detail: The functional equation and $\zeta_K(\sigma)\le\zeta(\sigma)^n$ for $\sigma>1$ give an upper bound of the shape $\mathrm{Res}\,\zeta_K\le(c\log d/n)^n$. Then $\log\mathrm{Res}\,\zeta_K\le n\log(c\log d/n)=o(\log d)$ when $n/\log d\to0$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\zeta_K/\zeta$ is entire when $K$ is Galois over $\mathbb Q$.
steps.detail: Write $\zeta_K$ as a product of Artin $L$-functions over the irreducible characters of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb Q)$. Brauer's induction theorem makes each $L$-function meromorphic, and Brauer's argument shows that the quotient $\zeta_K/\zeta$ has no poles.

steps.slogan: Bound the residue from below by Siegel's argument on a possible real zero near $1$.
steps.detail: Because $\zeta_K/\zeta$ is entire, Landau's lemma and Siegel's argument control a real zero of $\zeta_K$ near $1$. They give $\mathrm{Res}\,\zeta_K\ge d^{-\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$ once $d$ is large, so $\log\mathrm{Res}\,\zeta_K\ge-o(\log d)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds to get $\log(hR)\sim\log\sqrt d$.
steps.detail: The two bounds give $\log\mathrm{Res}\,\zeta_K=o(\log d)$. By the first step, $\log(hR)=(\tfrac12+o(1))\log d$, which is the claim.

concepts.c:number-field: The theorem concerns class numbers and regulators of number fields.
concepts.c:discriminant: The discriminant sets the size scale against which hR is compared.
concepts.c:regulator: The regulator enters through the product hR in the class number formula.
concepts.c:galois-extension: Galois fields allow the Artin L-function factorization of the zeta function.
concepts.c:dedekind-zeta-function: Its residue at 1 carries the class number and the regulator.

source.ref: R. Brauer, On the zeta-functions of algebraic number fields, American Journal of Mathematics 69 (1947), 243-250; see also S. Lang, Algebraic Number Theory, 2nd edition, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 110, Springer, 1994, chapter XVI
source.note: Siegel proved the quadratic case (Acta Arithmetica 1 (1935)); Brauer extended it to fields Galois over the rationals.

statement: There is a [spectrum](c:stable-homotopy-type) $I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}$ and a natural isomorphism $[X,I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}]\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_0X,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ for every spectrum $X$. So $[X,\Sigma^nI_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}]\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_nX,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is the [Pontryagin dual](c:pontryagin-dual) of $\pi_nX$.
conclusion: The cohomology theory $X\mapsto[X,\Sigma^nI_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}]$ is the Pontryagin dual of the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group-of-a-spectrum) $\pi_nX$.

proofs.name: Brown representability
proofs.slogan: The functor $\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_0X,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ is a Brown functor because $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is injective, so a spectrum represents it.
proofs.scope: The whole construction. No hypothesis restricts $X$: the proof works in the stable homotopy category of all spectra, and the shift step extends the case $n=0$ to all $n$.

steps.slogan: Define the contravariant functor $H(X)=\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_0X,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ on the homotopy category of spectra.
steps.detail: A map of spectra induces a map of $\pi_0$, and $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ reverses it. So $H$ is a contravariant functor from the homotopy category of [spectra](c:stable-homotopy-type) to abelian groups.

steps.slogan: Show that $H$ sends cofibre sequences to exact sequences.
steps.detail: The functor $\pi_0$ sends a cofibre sequence $X\to Y\to Z$ to an exact sequence. The group $\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z$ is [injective](c:injective-module), so $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ preserves exactness. Hence $H(Z)\to H(Y)\to H(X)$ is exact.

steps.slogan: Show that $H$ sends wedges of spectra to products of groups.
steps.detail: The group $\pi_0$ of a wedge is the direct sum of the $\pi_0$ of the summands. The functor $\mathrm{Hom}(-,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$ sends a direct sum to the product of the groups of homomorphisms.

steps.slogan: Apply Brown representability to the [Brown functor](c:brown-functor) $H$ to get the spectrum $I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}$.
steps.detail: The two previous steps say that $H$ is a cohomological functor that takes wedges to products. Brown representability gives a spectrum $I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}$ and a natural isomorphism $[X,I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}]\cong H(X)$.

steps.slogan: Shift $X$ to read off the dual of every homotopy group.
steps.detail: For every $n$, $[X,\Sigma^nI_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}]=[\Sigma^{-n}X,I_{\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z}]\cong\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_0\Sigma^{-n}X,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)=\mathrm{Hom}(\pi_nX,\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z)$. This is the [Pontryagin dual](c:pontryagin-dual) of $\pi_nX$.

concepts.c:stable-homotopy-type: The functor and the representing object live in the homotopy category of spectra.
concepts.c:pontryagin-dual: The represented theory takes each homotopy group to its Pontryagin dual.
concepts.c:homotopy-group-of-a-spectrum: These groups are dualized by the represented cohomology theory.
concepts.c:injective-module: Injectivity of Q/Z makes the functor Hom into it exact.
concepts.c:brown-functor: Brown representability applies because the functor sends wedges to products and is exact.

source.note: The construction of E. H. Brown and M. Comenetz, Pontrjagin duality for generalized homology and cohomology theories, American Journal of Mathematics 98 (1976); the proof is Brown representability for the dual functor.

statement: Let $X$ be a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) smooth $n$-[manifold](c:smooth-manifold) such that every [compact subset](c:compact-subspace) of $X$ lies in an open set diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$. Then $X$ is diffeomorphic to [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb R^n$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) smooth manifold of dimension $n$.
Every [compact subset](c:compact-subspace) of $X$ lies in an open subset diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$.

conclusion: The manifold $X$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$.

proofs.name: Exhaustion by smooth balls
proofs.slogan: Exhaust the manifold by nested smooth closed balls, show that the shells between them are products, and assemble the union into $\mathbb R^n$.
proofs.scope: The case $n\ge1$; for $n=0$ the hypothesis forces $X$ to be a point. The hypothesis also forces $X$ to be nonempty and connected.

roles.why: Paracompactness and connectedness give a countable exhaustion by compact sets, and the smooth structure gives collars.
Each compact piece of the exhaustion lies in a chart diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$, where a round ball contains it.

steps.slogan: Show that $X$ is connected and exhaust it by compact sets $L_1\subset L_2\subset\cdots$.
steps.detail: Any two points lie in a compact set, so in one open copy of $\mathbb R^n$, and $X$ is connected. A connected [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) manifold is second countable, so it has compact sets $L_j\subset\mathrm{int}\,L_{j+1}$ with union $X$.

steps.slogan: Choose closed smooth balls $B_1\subset\mathrm{int}\,B_2\subset\cdots$ with $L_j\subset B_j$.
steps.detail: Let $B_1$ be a round ball in a chart. Given $B_j$, the compact set $B_j\cup L_{j+1}$ lies in an open $U\cong\mathbb R^n$ by hypothesis, so a large round ball $B_{j+1}$ of $U$ contains it in its interior. Then $X=\bigcup_jB_j$.

steps.slogan: Show that each shell $B_{j+1}\setminus\mathrm{int}\,B_j$ is diffeomorphic to $S^{n-1}\times[0,1]$.
steps.detail: In $\mathrm{int}\,B_{j+1}\cong\mathbb R^n$ the ball $B_j$ and a small round ball are two embedded closed discs. By the Palais-Cerf disc theorem an [isotopy](c:isotopy) supported in $\mathrm{int}\,B_{j+1}$ carries one to the other, after a reflection if needed. So the shell is diffeomorphic to a round shell.

steps.slogan: Choose the shell diffeomorphisms to agree on collars so that they glue smoothly.
steps.detail: By uniqueness of collar neighbourhoods, the shell diffeomorphisms can be adjusted near each boundary sphere $\partial B_j$ to match a fixed collar from both sides. Then they fit together into one smooth map from $X\setminus\mathrm{int}\,B_1$ onto $S^{n-1}\times[1,\infty)$.

steps.slogan: Identify the union of the ball $B_1$ and the shells with $\mathbb R^n$.
steps.detail: The ball $B_1$ together with $S^{n-1}\times[1,\infty)$, glued along $\partial B_1\cong S^{n-1}$ with the radial structure, is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$ by $(x,r)\mapsto rx$. So $X\cong\mathbb R^n$.

concepts.c:paracompact-space: Paracompactness gives a countable exhaustion by compact sets.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The conclusion and the collars are statements about smooth structure.
concepts.c:compact-subspace: The hypothesis puts each compact piece inside a copy of Euclidean space.
concepts.c:euclidean-space: The charts and the final identification are with Euclidean space.
concepts.c:isotopy: An isotopy moves the inner ball onto a round ball without changing the outer one.

source.note: The classical argument for a monotone union of open cells (M. Brown, 1961), here in the smooth category with the Palais-Cerf disc theorem.
